candidates.title: Software factories and code reviews with Harjot Gill
candidates.author: Gergely Orosz (host); guest Harjot Gill, CodeRabbit CEO
candidates.organization: The Pragmatic Engineer (podcast episode + show notes)
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-18T18:08:52Z (confirmed via page datePublished; after Edition 2 send)
candidates.paywall: free (show notes, takeaways and transcript tab are public; 1:26:37 episode)
candidates.what_changed: A detailed, on-the-record account of a 'software factory' operating model at an AI dev-tools startup: ~5,000 agent-generated PRs/month by the CEO, ~$250-275K/month personal AI spend, human per-PR review replaced by release-level review plus a layered self-verification stack for agents, and a 'review exempt list' with an outage-strike system.
candidates.mechanism: Agents verify their own work ('hill climbing') through layers: (1) formal models (TLA+ found race conditions code review missed; now experimenting with Lean); (2) local deterministic simulation harness that fuzzes concurrent interleavings; (3) emulated real APIs (e.g. Google Cloud API mocks); (4) agent-spun dev environments on Google Cloud/Vercel; (5) production staged rollouts behind feature flags with an agent watching perf/logs and widening the rollout when stable. Humans review plans, final assets and releases (multiple PRs), not individual PRs. Devs on a 'review exempt list' push to prod unreviewed; an outage traced to their PR earns a 'strike', and enough strikes revokes the exemption. Much of the PR volume is 'janitorial' (CI, flaky tests, caching).
candidates.evidence_quality: Self-reported practitioner testimony in an interview (single company, CEO who sells AI code review). No independent metrics on defect rates, incident rates or quality. Numbers are internally inconsistent across sources: the post says 5,000+ PRs last month at ~$250-275K/month and 'around $150' per PR, but $250K / 5,000 = ~$50/PR; Gill's own Oct 2026 tweets cited in the notes say ~3,000 PRs/month at ~$200K and '5K PRs last week' for the whole CodeRabbit team. Treat per-PR cost as UNVERIFIED. Orosz flags CodeRabbit as an outlier (typical spend he hears: $200-$2,000/dev/month).
candidates.independent_confirmation: None for the quality/cost claims. Orosz links the cost discussion to his Nov 17 inference deepdive (already used in Edition 2) on KV-cache economics ($200/month Max plans ~ $8,000-14,000/month of API-equivalent usage). Gill's dotfiles are public: https://github.com/coderabbitai/dotfiles (not read).
candidates.relevance: High for practitioners: a concrete, copyable verification ladder for agent-written code (formal spec -> deterministic simulation -> API emulation -> dev deploy -> agent-monitored staged rollout), and a governance pattern (review-exempt list + strikes) as an alternative to per-PR review. Also a cost-per-shipped-change data point for the 'cost per solved task' thread.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 2's harness-enforced checks, judges vs rule checks and cost-per-solved-task themes, and to the Nov 17 Pragmatic Engineer inference deepdive (used). New angle: release-level review and the layered self-verification stack. Not in ed2_urls.txt.
candidates.summary: Orosz interviews CodeRabbit founder/CEO Harjot Gill (AI code review company, ~40 engineers, 'millions of dollars per month' company AI spend). Gill says he shipped 5,000+ PRs last month using agents, much of it during commutes and nights, at a personal AI spend of ~$250-275K/month; the post says a PR costs him 'around $150' (note: this does not reconcile with $250K/5,000 PRs = ~$50; and his own cited October tweet says ~3,000 PRs/month at ~$200K tokens). Much of the volume is janitorial: CI improvements, fixing flaky tests, refining caching, UI polish. Agent-built artifacts named: a Rust write-ahead log on top of object stores (agent ran for six weeks; now in production), migration of all services to Bun over a weekend, and a new CI system built in about a week after being quoted $13M/year for a CI vendor solution; the in-house CI cost ~50% less than the quote with similar performance. Verification ladder ('agents must hill climb'): TLA+ (caught race conditions that code review missed), Lean experiments, a deterministic simulation harness fuzzing concurrent interleavings, emulated cloud APIs, agent-deployed dev environments (Google Cloud, Vercel), and feature-flagged progressive rollouts where an agent watches performance and logs and continues the rollout when stable (Orosz compares to OpenAI's 'Perf Factory'). Review: 'human code review is dead' for agent code; engineers review plans and releases (bundles of PRs). A 'review exempt list' lets trusted devs push to prod without review; outages are traced to the causing PR and the author gets a strike; enough strikes and their releases require peer review. CodeRabbit stopped fine-tuning its review models because frontier models improve too fast to keep fine-tunes competitive. 'War rooms' of eng/product/design steer agents together to go from prototype to working product. Hiring ad asked for candidates with 1,000+ non-slop PRs in the last 30 days or 500+ hours of strategy games (Civilization, Factorio, etc.). Gill reports disturbed sleep (waking at night to nudge agents) - Orosz calls it the 'Dracula effect'. Orosz's caveats: CodeRabbit is an outlier whose AI spend functions as R&D for products it sells; typical per-dev spend he hears is $200-$2,000/month; open models could cut much of the spend at some capability cost. Timestamps include 25:37 'What's replacing human code review', 38:44 'Technical debt and deslopping tests', 46:05 'Evals', 50:25 'Formal methods', 52:05 'AI cost at CodeRabbit'. Sponsor note: episode sponsored by turbopuffer, Entire and WorkOS (Airlock agent authorization).

candidates.title: Agentic inference capacity grew 4.6× in a year, versus 2.6× for compute capacity
candidates.author: Jason Li
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-18 (confirmed via page datePublished; date-only, so may predate the ~09:00 UTC Edition 2 send, but URL not in Edition 2)
candidates.what_changed: First application of Epoch's Inference Performance Index (IPI, introduced Nov 9) to its AI Chip Sales dataset: installed agentic-inference capacity grew 4.6× (Q2 2025 -> Q2 2026) vs 2.6× for peak 8-bit FLOP/s, i.e. FLOP/s understates growth in serving capacity for long-context, cached agent workloads.
candidates.mechanism: Per-chip IPI scores (v1, in GB300-equivalents) measured on a fixed basket of agentic workloads with long cached contexts, accounting for memory, inter-chip communication and lower precision, both prefill and decode; multiplied by cumulative chips sold per family and summed. Growth is driven mostly by the Hopper-to-Blackwell transition: GB300 ~8× the inference capacity of H200 per GPU vs only ~2.2× from GB300 to Vera Rubin VR200 (modeled).
candidates.evidence_quality: Modeled estimate with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals (90% UI 4.2-5.1× inference, 2.5-2.7× peak compute). Key judgment assumptions: 60/40 GB-NVL72 vs B/HGX split, even H100/H200 split from Q4 2024. Software efficiency not modeled; UI excludes uncertainty in modeled per-chip performance.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None independent; builds on Epoch's own IPI report (Nov 9) and AI Chip Sales dataset.
candidates.relevance: Medium: useful context for inference economics and why prefix/KV caching and memory bandwidth matter more than FLOP/s for agent serving; ties to Edition 2's prefix-caching and inference-economics thread. Not directly actionable.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to Edition 2 prefix caching / Pragmatic Engineer inference deepdive; URL not previously used.
candidates.summary: Between Q2 2025 and Q2 2026 the estimated agentic inference capacity of all AI chips sold to date grew 4.6× while peak 8-bit compute grew 2.6× (total ~6.67M GB300e in Q2 2026 vs ~1.45M in Q2 2025; peak compute ~3.2e7 vs 1.2e7 H100e). Blackwell + Blackwell Ultra account for 74% of added capacity and ~73% of total agentic inference capacity by Q2 2026 vs 50% of peak compute. GB300 delivers ~8× H200 inference capacity per GPU. Inference capacity per unit of peak compute rose ~77% over the year ('hardware-model co-design': bigger scale-up domains, lower precision, architectures that use hardware better). Chips sold in Q2 2026 added 3.3× the capacity of those sold in Q2 2025, below the 4.6× total, so Epoch expects growth to slow; regression of log additions gives 3.2×/yr for inference capacity and 2.1×/yr for peak compute (Q1 2024-Q2 2026 window: 6.8× and 2.5×/yr, doubling times 4.3 and 9.2 months). Sustaining 4.6× would need annual additions of 3.6× the starting base. Modeled gain GB300 -> VR200 is only 2.2× per GPU. Sensitivity: 90% UI 4.2-5.1× (inference) and 2.5-2.7× (peak); earlier H200 transition scenario gives 4.5×. Limitations: judgment-based rack/server split, H100/H200 split, no software efficiency modelling.

candidates.title: Anthropic's compute spending is increasing by 4x per year, outpacing OpenAI's 3x
candidates.author: Josh You
candidates.event_date: Data through Q3 2026, from Anthropic S-1/A filed 2026-11-02
candidates.what_changed: Epoch compiles Anthropic's S-1/A compute-and-infrastructure disclosures into run rates: ~$9.86B in Q3 2026 (~$39.5B annualized), up from $433M in 2023, ~4×/yr growth; OpenAI ~3×/yr from sparser media reports.
candidates.mechanism: Quarterly and annual spend converted to annualized run rates; Anthropic from SEC filings (S-1/A), OpenAI from Fortune, The Information and Reuters (Brockman testimony of ~$50B 2026 compute plan, a forecast).
candidates.evidence_quality: Anthropic figures: primary SEC filing (strong). OpenAI figures: media reports and forecasts (weaker), so the 'outpacing' comparison is less certain - Epoch says so.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Underlying Anthropic numbers come from the public S-1/A (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm, not read in this slice).
candidates.relevance: Low for 'try this week' practitioners; industry economics context (compute supply, possible pricing pressure). Brief or Research-corner material at most.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: None direct; tangential to Edition 2 inference economics.
candidates.summary: Anthropic compute & infrastructure spend (S-1/A): 2023 $433M; 2024 $2.522B; Q1 2025 $944M ($3.78B annualized); Q2 2025 $1.39B; Q3 2025 $2.047B; Q4 2025 $2.945B ($11.78B ann.); Q1 2026 $3.387B; Q2 2026 $5.558B ($22.23B ann.); Q3 2026 $9.863B ($39.45B ann.). Roughly 4×/year. OpenAI: 2022 $416M (incl. some data costs), 2024 $5.8B ($1.8B inference + $4.0B R&D compute, projection), 2025 $16.3B ($8.0B inference + $8.3B R&D), 2026 ~$50B forecast (Brockman, May 2026) - about 3×/yr. Anthropic paid SpaceX ~ $5B for compute in Q3 2026, roughly half its quarterly compute spend. S-1 discloses $447.5B of commitments, 'substantially all' compute and infrastructure, from Sept 2026 through 2030 (~$100B/yr). Most spending at both labs goes to cloud partners (Amazon, Google, Microsoft, SpaceX).
